title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
keywords: avoiding state changes through unsafe get requests
subtopics: Avoiding state changes through unsafe GET requests.
learning_outcomes: Explain what cross-site request forgery contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: csrf threat model.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Security begins at trust boundaries. Validate data for the intended operation, encode output for its exact context, constrain file and network access, protect credentials, and apply authorization consistently. In this lesson, focus on csrf threat model; then compare it with token-based defenses. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use cross-site request forgery when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Security begins at trust boundaries. Validate data for the intended operation, encode output for its exact context, constrain file and network access, protect credentials, and apply authorization consistently. For cross-site request forgery, begin with csrf threat model. Also distinguish token-based defenses; samesite cookies; origin and request validation. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: CSRF threat model
items.text: Treat the relevant value as untrusted, apply the defense at the correct boundary, and verify a deliberately invalid or hostile-looking input is rejected or encoded.

items.title: Token-based defenses
items.text: Distinguish identity verification from resource permission, and test expiry, invalid credentials, and denied access as well as the success path.

items.title: SameSite cookies
items.text: Know when to use samesite cookies, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Origin and request validation
items.text: Track where this value enters the request lifecycle and where it affects the response; client-provided data must be treated as untrusted.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating input validation as output escaping.
common_mistakes.why: A value can be valid data and still be unsafe in an HTML or JavaScript output context.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate shape and business rules at input boundaries, then apply context-appropriate output encoding.

common_mistakes.why: A request can be sent without the original form or browser UI.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat all security-relevant validation and authorization on the server.

common_mistakes.problem: Returning internal error details to the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Stack traces and configuration values may expose sensitive information.
common_mistakes.fix: Log safe diagnostics server-side and return a generic, useful response.
